title: Multivariable Calculus
body:
[[Partial Derivative]]
[[Multiple Integration]]
[[Gradient]]

---

Calculus where the input is a point rather than a number. [[CALCULUS 1]] differentiated
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$; here $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a surface (or a
hypersurface), and the single question "what is the slope" splits into "the slope in which
direction".

That split is the whole subject:

- One direction at a time gives a [[Partial Derivative]]
- All the coordinate directions bundled together gives the [[Gradient]], and dotting it with a unit
  vector answers for **any** direction
- Composing dependencies gives the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]], a sum over paths rather than a
  single product
- Setting the gradient to zero gives [[Multivariable Optimization]], where the new phenomenon is
  the saddle point, and [[Lagrange Multipliers]] when there is a constraint
- Integrating in several variables gives [[Multiple Integration]], done one variable at a time

**Nothing here is a new technique.** Every partial is an ordinary derivative from
[[Differentiation Rules]] with the other letters treated as constants, and every iterated integral
is an ordinary integral from [[Integration Techniques]]. What is new is the bookkeeping: which
variable is held fixed, which paths a dependence takes, and what the limits of the inner integral
are.

[[CALCULUS 2]] introduces this block and hands it here; [[Vector Calculus]] is the other half of
this course, where the *output* becomes a vector too.
